source.title_on_document: Can ChatGPT enhance business student creativity? Evidence from a randomised controlled trial

supplement.where: No supplementary material or online appendix is mentioned in the saved article, and none is included in the PDF (PDF pp. 1-16).
supplement.holds: No supplementary contents are described. The reported statistics are in the main text and Tables 1-2 (PDF pp. 9-10); analyzed participant counts, per-arm counts, and labeled standard deviations are not provided.

paper_design_summary: First-year business undergraduates were randomly assigned within discipline, before class, to ChatGPT-3.5 or no generative AI during a 15-minute in-class task: paperclip uses for Entrepreneurship and Marketing, or ideas to return employees to the workplace for Management (PDF pp. 7-8). The reported recruitment total of 1190 across 26 classes includes enrollments in multiple subjects; counts of distinct people randomized and analyzed are not printed (PDF pp. 7-10). Three raters scored submitted ideas for fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration; flexibility was dropped, and the paper reports a 2 x 2 group-by-discipline MANOVA for Entrepreneurship and Marketing and a separate Management MANOVA (PDF pp. 8-10).

participants.exclusions: The paper reports recruited enrollments of Entrepreneurship n = 160 (3 elective classes) and Marketing n = 496 (12 core classes), not counts explicitly recorded at randomization (PDF p. 7). These discipline totals are not confirmed counts of distinct people: duplicates from students attending two subjects were removed, without identifying all affected subject pairs or the number removed. Incomplete data and submissions from non-consenting students were excluded (PDF p. 8). The pre-processing section covering both MANOVAs reports removal of outliers after non-normal residuals (number not stated), followed by two multivariate outliers; it does not allocate those two cases to S1 or S2 (PDF p. 9). Attendance, consent, exclusion counts by arm, and exact numbers analyzed are not printed. The S1 univariate residual df = 198 provide evidence for the eligibility threshold, but no inferred analyzed count is entered (PDF pp. 9-10).

ai_tool.how_used: Experiment-group students used ChatGPT-3.5 freely during the 15-minute task, with prompts they wrote themselves. Before the task, all participants in both groups received guidance on using ChatGPT-3.5 for ideation and watched a 2-minute video on prompting it. Responses were submitted to a non-graded item in the Learning Management System (PDF p. 7-8).

task.description: Alternative Uses Test variant: list uses for a paperclip. Done in class, administered by a researcher who was not the class teacher, and submitted through a non-graded item in the Learning Management System.

outcomes.name: Fluency (total number of ideas generated)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of the total number of ideas each respondent generated, recorded by each of the three raters; inter-rater r = .83-.95 (PDF p. 8). How the three raters' counts were combined is not stated. The paper calls fluency 'the primary index of creative ideation' when it justifies dropping flexibility (PDF p. 9); this is not read as naming a primary outcome. Analyzed in the 2 x 2 MANOVA with originality and elaboration, followed by univariate tests and pairwise comparisons by discipline.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1: students were explicitly randomly assigned within discipline, before class, to ChatGPT-3.5 assistance or a control instructed not to use generative AI (PDF p. 7, 'Description of participants and sampling' and 'Measures and procedures'). Criterion 2: exact analyzed person counts are unreported, so all randomized and analyzed count fields remain null. The recruitment totals are not used to establish this criterion. S1 analyzes per-respondent submissions in a 2 x 2 between-student MANOVA, with repeated univariate residual df = 198 and multivariate F(3, 196) (PDF p. 8, outcome definitions; PDF pp. 9-10, Results). With three raters assessing each student's submission, S1 exceeds 50 distinct analyzed people even if their ratings had been entered separately; this is a threshold check, not a reported sample count. S1 therefore establishes paper-level eligibility without relying on the exact S2 sample size. Criterion 3: raters counted and evaluated the ideas students submitted during the task, with ChatGPT-3.5 available to the experiment arm; fluency, originality, and elaboration are scored on output (PDF pp. 7-8, 'Measures and procedures').

one_line_finding: ChatGPT-3.5 raised fluency (control 2.52 vs ChatGPT 3.65), originality (0.79 vs 1.14), and elaboration (0.80 vs 1.50) for Marketing students, raised fluency (1.78 vs 2.29) and elaboration (1.06 vs 1.99) but not originality (0.66 vs 0.77, p = .064) for Management students, and made no detectable difference for Entrepreneurship students (Tables 1-2, PDF p. 10).
open_questions: S1 pooled univariate labels remain uncertain: the text attributes F(1,198) = 0.14 for fluency, F(1,198) = 25.62 for originality, and F(1, 198) = 0.001 for elaboration to intervention, whereas the earlier reconciliation questioned these labels using Table 1. The source prints no correction (PDF pp. 9-10). Author-provided MANOVA output would settle the labels; retain printed values and use per-discipline contrasts until then.

Exact numbers of distinct people randomized and analyzed, the number attending or consenting, and attrition by reason are unreported. The paper's 1190 and discipline recruitment counts (160, 496, 534) precede duplicate removal and other exclusions (PDF pp. 7-9). S1's reported residual df establish the paper-level 50-person threshold without supplying an exact analyzed count; the missing flow counts still require author clarification.

Exact analyzed counts by arm and discipline are absent from Tables 1-2 (PDF p. 10). Do not reconstruct person counts from rounded, unlabeled parenthetical values. Counts remain null pending author-provided participant flow and analysis sample information.

Tables 1-2 give unlabeled parenthetical values, so the source does not establish whether they are standard errors or standard deviations (PDF p. 10). The earlier standard-error interpretation is unconfirmed and is not used to code a precision value. Authors would need to identify the statistic and supply participant-level dispersion if unavailable.

Management reporting inconsistencies remain: Wilks Lambda = .07 is printed with F(3, 118) = 19.92 and partial η² = .33; originality uses F(1,198), whereas fluency and elaboration use residual df = 120 (PDF p. 10). The Results also describe the second, Management MANOVA as including 'Discipline (Entrepreneurship vs Marketing)' as its only independent variable (PDF p. 9). Original analysis output from the authors would settle these apparent errors; no replacement statistic is coded.

The rule for combining the three raters' scores, the numeric coding of the 5-point rubric, and the blinding protocol are not stated. Originality inter-rater r = .32-.49 (PDF p. 8); the Discussion mentions identifying AI-assisted ideas from the quantity of responses (PDF p. 11). Author-provided scoring instructions and analysis code would settle these measurement details. Output-based scoring is explicit; S1 meets the paper-level people threshold even without settling aggregation.

Randomization mechanics and allocation communication are not described beyond assignment of students within discipline before class (PDF p. 7). The explicit random-assignment statement supports criterion 1; an author-provided protocol would settle risk-of-bias details.

Final coding review retains two study entries following the separate task analyses; idea_generation for the Management workplace problem; field_rct for tasks conducted in regular classes; and ai_vs_bau because internet searches were permitted among usual control resources rather than assigned as a separate intervention (PDF pp. 7-9; codebook sections 4-6). These classification choices require no additional source and do not change eligibility.
notes: Coded as two studies that follow the paper's two MANOVAs: S1 = Entrepreneurship and Marketing (paperclip task, 2 x 2 MANOVA), S2 = Management (return-to-workplace task, one-way MANOVA). The paper describes one trial with randomization stratified by discipline. The paper reports duplicate removal across subjects, but does not describe which record was retained or count the removals. Recruitment counts are discipline enrollments and can include the same student in more than one subject. Each multivariate test is recorded once per study, under fluency (the S1-O1 combined contrast and S2-O1), labeled as the joint test of all three outcomes. Other S1 multivariate results (PDF p. 9): discipline main effect, Pillai's trace 0.19, F(3, 196) = 15.31, p < .001, partial η² = .19; intervention x discipline interaction, Pillai's trace = .09, F(3, 196) = 6.75, p < .001, partial η² = .09. Box's M was significant for the first MANOVA, so Pillai's trace is reported there. Design is coded field_rct because the task ran inside the students' ordinary classes (26 classes), though a researcher who was not the teacher ran it as a non-graded research task. The control group could use internet searches and other usual resources, so the comparison is ai_vs_bau. All participants, control included, received the ChatGPT-3.5 guidance and prompting video. No outcome is named primary: the sentence that calls fluency 'the primary index of creative ideation' justifies keeping fluency over flexibility. Per-discipline contrasts in Table 1 print means, unlabeled parentheticals, and p-values only. No preregistration, data, or code is mentioned; ethics approval is stated (PDF p. 8). Finalization checked the complete markdown and the relevant PDF pages. Recruitment figures are retained only as recruitment figures; exact randomized and analyzed counts remain null. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as audit history, including its superseded randomized-count decision and earlier numerical reconstructions. Current eligibility uses S1's reported degrees of freedom only to establish the 50-person threshold. No unreported sample size, arm size, corrected test statistic, standard error, or standard deviation is entered as a confirmed value.

differences.a: One study (S1) covering all three disciplines, with per-discipline contrasts and one task entry that holds both tasks
differences.b: Two studies: S1 Entrepreneurship and Marketing (paperclip task, first MANOVA); S2 Management (return-to-workplace task, second MANOVA)
differences.resolved: Two studies, as in B. The paper analyzes the Management students in a separate MANOVA because they did a different task, and after duplicate removal the two analyses use different students. The codebook gives experiments on separate samples their own entries. The paper's one-trial framing and shared randomization protocol are recorded in notes, and Review 1 can merge the studies.

agreed_fields_checked.value: Both forms describe the 2-minute prompting video as part of the ChatGPT arm only. The source says all participants, control included, received identical instructions and the video. Corrected in the final arm descriptions and how_used.

agreed_fields_checked.value: ai_vs_bau. The control group used its usual resources, which could include internet searches, and was told not to use generative AI. No alternative aid was assigned.
agreed_fields_checked.quote: In the Control Group, students generated ideas independently using their usual resources, such as discipline materials, personal knowledge, or internet searches. They were explicitly instructed not to use any generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, during the task.

agreed_fields_checked.value: field_rct. The task ran in the students' ordinary classes (26 classes) as a non-graded LMS item, run by a researcher who was not the class teacher. A lab_rct reading is possible; both codes are core.

reconciliation.notes: Both raw forms parsed. All seven differences were settled from the source. Checks of agreed fields found one shared error (both arms watched the prompting video, PDF p. 8) and one reporting problem in the paper itself (the combined Entrepreneurship+Marketing follow-up F values match Table 1's discipline effects, not the intervention effects).

open_items.item: open_questions[0]: S1 pooled univariate effect labels need the authors' original MANOVA output (PDF pp. 9-10). This affects effect extraction, not random assignment, the S1 people threshold, or output-based scoring.

open_questions[1]: Exact distinct-person assignment and analysis counts and attrition flow require author confirmation (PDF pp. 7-10). S1's reported residual df and per-respondent scoring already establish the paper-level 50-person threshold; these missing exact counts do not block core inclusion.

open_questions[2]: Exact analyzed counts by arm and discipline require the authors' analysis sample information (PDF p. 10, Tables 1-2). They are needed for extraction and attrition assessment; the eligibility rule counts all arms of S1.

open_questions[3]: Authors must identify the unlabeled parenthetical statistics and any participant-level dispersion in Tables 1-2 (PDF p. 10). Missing precision affects pooling, not the three screening criteria.

open_questions[4]: Apparent Management MANOVA label, Wilks Lambda, and originality-df errors require original author analysis output (PDF pp. 9-10). S1 independently establishes the paper's eligibility.

open_questions[5]: Rater aggregation, scale coding, and blinding require the authors' scoring protocol or analysis code (PDF pp. 8 and 11). Outcomes are explicitly scored on submissions, and S1 remains above the people threshold even if rater records were separate.

open_questions[6]: Authors could supply randomization and allocation procedures for risk-of-bias assessment (PDF p. 7). Explicit random assignment to ChatGPT access or no generative AI already meets criterion 1.

open_questions[7]: Two-study structure, Management task type, field_rct, and ai_vs_bau are settled coding choices under the source and current codebook (PDF pp. 7-9). No additional evidence is needed for eligibility.

Challenge follow-up: Which analysis lost either of the two multivariate outliers is not reported (PDF p. 9). Authors could provide the exclusion log; the missing allocation does not affect S1's already reported post-exclusion df or core eligibility.
